# Chapter 3: Implementation Techniques for Agent Memory

> **Key Insight**: The difference between a memory system that works in a demo and one that works in production is not the architecture — it is the implementation details. Embedding quality, chunking strategy, retrieval tuning, and compression discipline determine whether your agent remembers what matters and forgets what does not.

## Why Implementation Details Matter

Chapter 1 established what agent memory is and why it matters. Chapter 2 will explore the architectural patterns for combining memory types into coherent systems. This chapter focuses on the concrete techniques you use to build those systems: how to choose and configure embedding models, how to select and tune a vector database, how to design retrieval pipelines that return the right memories, and how to compress and consolidate memories so your system scales.

These are not academic questions. The choice between cosine similarity and dot product, between fixed-size chunking and semantic chunking, between extractive and abstractive summarization — each decision has measurable effects on retrieval quality, latency, and cost. This chapter gives you the technical grounding to make those decisions deliberately rather than by default.

## Vector-Based Memory

Vector-based memory is the dominant approach to long-term agent memory. The core idea is simple: convert text into numerical vectors (embeddings) that capture semantic meaning, store those vectors in a database optimized for similarity search, and retrieve the most similar vectors when the agent needs relevant information.

The simplicity of the idea belies the complexity of the implementation. Every component in the pipeline — the embedding model, the vector database, the similarity metric, the chunking strategy — involves trade-offs that affect the system's behavior.

### Embedding Models for Memory

The embedding model is the foundation of vector-based memory. It determines how well semantic similarity is captured, which in turn determines retrieval quality. No embedding model is universally best; the right choice depends on your domain, language requirements, and performance constraints.

#### Text Embedding Models

The most common use case is embedding natural language text. Several families of models dominate this space:

- **OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and text-embedding-3-large**: Proprietary models with strong performance across domains. The small variant (1536 dimensions) offers good quality at low cost; the large variant (3072 dimensions) provides marginally better quality for demanding applications. Both support 8192-token inputs.
- **BGE (BAAI General Embedding)**: Open-source models that consistently rank among the best on benchmark suites. BGE-m3 supports 100+ languages and multiple granularities (token, sentence, passage) in a single model. Available in base (768D) and large (1024D) variants.
- **E5 (Embedding by E5)**: Another strong open-source family from Microsoft. E5-mistral combines a Mistral backbone with embedding heads for high-quality multilingual embeddings.
- **Cohere embed-v3**: Proprietary model with strong multilingual support and configurable input types (search_document, search_query, classification, clustering).
- **Nomic-embed**: Open-source models optimized for cost-effective deployment. The text-v1.5 variant (768D) performs well on general-domain tasks.

When choosing a text embedding model, consider:

| Factor | Guidance |
|--------|----------|
| Dimensionality | Higher dimensions (1024-3072) capture more nuance but increase storage and computation. 768D is a practical sweet spot for most applications. |
| Language support | If your agent operates in multiple languages, choose a model with demonstrated multilingual performance (BGE-m3, Cohere embed-v3). |
| Input length | Most models support 512-8192 tokens. Longer inputs require chunking before embedding. |
| Cost | Open-source models (BGE, E5) eliminate per-token API costs but require GPU infrastructure. Proprietary models (OpenAI, Cohere) charge per token but require no infrastructure. |
| Latency | Embedding latency typically ranges from 10-100ms per document depending on model size and infrastructure. Batch embedding reduces per-document latency significantly. |

#### Code Embedding Models

Agents that interact with code need embeddings that capture code semantics — not just the text of code, but its structure, intent, and behavior. General-purpose text embeddings perform poorly on code because code has different syntactic and semantic properties than natural language.

- **CodeBERT**: A BERT model pre-trained on code-text pairs. Effective for code search and completion but limited to relatively short sequences (512 tokens).
- **StarCoder-based embeddings**: Models derived from the StarCoder code generation family, fine-tuned for embedding. Handle longer sequences and multiple programming languages.
- **Source2Vec**: Uses subword tokenization and doc2vec-style training to create embeddings that capture code semantics at the token, function, and file levels.
- **OpenAI text-embedding-3 models**: While not code-specific, they perform reasonably well on code due to their training data including code. A practical choice when you want a single model for both text and code.

For agents that primarily work with code, a dedicated code embedding model is worth the complexity. For agents that handle mixed text and code, a general-purpose model with code in its training data is often sufficient.

#### Multimodal Embedding Models

Some agents process images, audio, or other non-text inputs alongside text. Multimodal embedding models map different modalities into a shared vector space, enabling cross-modal retrieval.

- **CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training)**: The most widely used multimodal model. Maps images and text into a shared 512D or 768D space. OpenCLIP provides open-source implementations.
- **SigLIP**: Google's successor to CLIP, using sigmoid loss for better calibration. Available in multiple sizes.
- **OpenAI CLIP-based models**: Proprietary multimodal embeddings through the OpenAI API.

Multimodal embeddings are still an emerging area for agent memory. They are most useful for agents that need to retrieve visual information (e.g., a design review agent that references past screenshots) or that process mixed modalities in their inputs.

### Vector Database Options

The vector database is where embeddings are stored and queried. The choice of vector database affects performance, scalability, operational complexity, and feature availability.

| Database | Deployment | Key Strengths | Best For | Limitations |
|----------|------------|---------------|----------|-------------|
| **Pinecone** | Managed cloud | Serverless scaling, hybrid search, metadata filtering, low ops overhead | Production deployments where you want to avoid infrastructure management | Vendor lock-in; cost scales with usage; limited customization |
| **Weaviate** | Self-hosted or cloud | Hybrid search (vector + BM25), GraphQL API, multi-tenancy, module ecosystem | Complex schemas with rich metadata; teams that want GraphQL |
| **Chroma** | Embedded or cloud | Simple Python API, local-first design, zero-config setup | Prototyping, small deployments, local development |
| **FAISS** | Library (Meta) | Extremely fast similarity search, GPU acceleration, many index types | Research, custom pipelines, maximum performance control |
| **Qdrant** | Self-hosted or cloud | Rich filtering on payloads, Rust-based performance, REST and gRPC APIs | Applications requiring complex metadata filtering alongside vector search |
| **Milvus** | Self-hosted or cloud | Distributed architecture, cloud-native, many index types, active development | Large-scale deployments requiring horizontal scaling |
| **pgvector** | PostgreSQL extension | SQL integration, ACID transactions, familiar tooling | Teams already using PostgreSQL; applications needing relational + vector |

#### Decision Framework

Choose your vector database based on these factors:

1. **Scale**: For collections under 100K vectors, Chroma or FAISS are sufficient. For millions of vectors, consider Pinecone, Qdrant, or Milvus.
2. **Filtering needs**: If you need complex metadata filtering (e.g., "find memories from user X in the last week with tag Y"), Qdrant and Weaviate excel. FAISS has no built-in filtering.
3. **Operational overhead**: If you want zero infrastructure management, Pinecone is the simplest. If you prefer self-hosting, Qdrant and Weaviate are mature options.
4. **Hybrid search**: If you need keyword + vector search, Weaviate, Qdrant, and Pinecone support it natively. With FAISS or Chroma, you need to implement hybrid search yourself.
5. **Ecosystem**: If you are already using PostgreSQL, pgvector integrates seamlessly. If you are building a Python-first application, Chroma has the most Pythonic API.

### Similarity Search Strategies

Once embeddings are stored, the vector database must find the most similar vectors to a query. The similarity metric and the search algorithm both affect results.

#### Similarity Metrics

- **Cosine similarity**: Measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring magnitude. This is the most common metric for text embeddings because it is invariant to vector length. Values range from -1 (opposite) to 1 (identical), with 0 meaning orthogonal (unrelated).

- **Dot product**: The raw inner product of two vectors. Faster to compute than cosine similarity but sensitive to vector magnitude. When embeddings are L2-normalized (unit length), dot product equals cosine similarity. Many vector databases use dot product internally for efficiency.

- **Euclidean distance (L2)**: Measures the straight-line distance between vectors. Rarely used for text embeddings because it is sensitive to magnitude and does not capture directional similarity well. More common for image embeddings where absolute position in the vector space matters.

For text-based agent memory, cosine similarity (or dot product on normalized vectors) is the standard choice. Use Euclidean distance only if your embedding model's documentation specifically recommends it.

#### Search Algorithms

- **Flat (brute force)**: Compares the query vector against every stored vector. Exact but slow — O(n) comparisons. Only practical for small collections (under ~10K vectors).

- **HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)**: An approximate nearest neighbor algorithm that builds a multi-layer graph. Offers an excellent balance of speed and accuracy. Most vector databases use HNSW as their default index. Parameters `ef_construction` (build quality) and `ef_search` (query quality) control the accuracy-speed trade-off.

- **IVF (Inverted File Index)**: Partitions the vector space into clusters and searches only the most relevant clusters. Faster than HNSW for very large datasets but less accurate. Useful when you have millions of vectors and can tolerate some approximation.

- **PQ (Product Quantization)**: Compresses vectors by splitting them into sub-vectors and quantizing each independently. Dramatically reduces storage at the cost of accuracy. Useful for extremely large collections where storage cost is a constraint.

For most agent memory applications, HNSW with default parameters provides sufficient accuracy. Tune `ef_search` higher if you notice relevant memories being missed; tune it lower if query latency is too high.

### Chunking Strategies for Memory Storage

Before text can be embedded, it must be divided into chunks that fit within the embedding model's input length. Chunking is not a mechanical preprocessing step — it is a design decision that fundamentally affects retrieval quality.

#### Fixed-Size Chunking

The simplest approach: split text into fixed-size chunks (e.g., 512 tokens) with optional overlap (e.g., 50 tokens). This is easy to implement and predictable, but it often splits semantic units — a single idea may be divided across two chunks, reducing the quality of each chunk's embedding.

```python
# Fixed-size chunking with overlap
def chunk_fixed(text: str, chunk_size: int = 512, overlap: int = 50):
    """Split text into fixed-size chunks with overlap."""
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        end = start + chunk_size
        chunks.append(text[start:end])
        start = end - overlap
    return chunks
```

#### Recursive Chunking

A more sophisticated approach: split text by a hierarchy of separators (paragraphs, then sentences, then words) until chunks are small enough. This preserves more semantic structure because it respects natural text boundaries.

LangChain's `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` implements this pattern:

```python
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=512,
    chunk_overlap=50,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""]
)
chunks = splitter.split_text(long_document)
```

#### Semantic Chunking

The most advanced approach: use embeddings to identify natural boundaries in the text. Compute embeddings for consecutive sentences, measure the similarity between adjacent sentences, and split where similarity drops below a threshold. This produces chunks that are semantically coherent but requires computing embeddings during preprocessing.

```python
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

def semantic_chunk(sentences: list[str], model, threshold: float = 0.7):
    """Split sentences into chunks based on semantic similarity."""
    embeddings = model.encode(sentences)
    chunks = [[sentences[0]]]
    for i in range(1, len(sentences)):
        similarity = np.dot(embeddings[i], embeddings[i-1]) / (
            np.linalg.norm(embeddings[i]) * np.linalg.norm(embeddings[i-1])
        )
        if similarity < threshold:
            chunks.append([sentences[i]])
        else:
            chunks[-1].append(sentences[i])
    return [" ".join(chunk) for chunk in chunks]
```

#### Choosing a Chunking Strategy

| Strategy | Quality | Complexity | Best For |
|----------|---------|------------|----------|
| Fixed-size | Moderate | Low | Quick prototypes, uniform documents |
| Recursive | Good | Low | General-purpose, mixed document types |
| Semantic | Best | High | High-quality retrieval, homogeneous documents |
| Document-aware | Good | Medium | Structured documents (Markdown, HTML) |

For most agent memory applications, recursive chunking with 512-token chunks and 50-token overlap provides the best balance of quality and simplicity. Use semantic chunking when retrieval quality is critical and you can afford the preprocessing cost.

## Retrieval Techniques

Retrieval is the process of finding relevant memories for the agent's current task. It is the most impactful component of a memory system: even perfectly stored memories are useless if they cannot be found. This section covers the techniques for building retrieval pipelines that return the right memories, in the right order, at the right time.

### Semantic Search vs. Keyword Search vs. Hybrid

#### Semantic Search

Semantic search uses vector similarity to find memories that are meaningfully related to the query, even if they share no exact words. This is the strength of vector-based memory: it captures paraphrasing, synonyms, and conceptual relationships.

The weakness of pure semantic search is that it can miss exact matches. If the agent queries for "API key rotation policy," a semantically similar document about "credential management" might be returned instead of the exact policy document. Semantic search also struggles with proper nouns, version numbers, and other precise identifiers.

#### Keyword Search

Keyword search (typically BM25) finds memories that contain the exact terms in the query. It is fast, precise, and excellent for finding specific terms — but it cannot handle paraphrasing or synonyms. A query for "how to reset password" will not match a document that says "restoring account access."

#### Hybrid Search

Hybrid search combines semantic and keyword scores, typically as a weighted sum:

```
final_score = α × semantic_score + (1 - α) × keyword_score
```

where α controls the balance (commonly 0.7 for semantic-heavy, 0.5 for equal weight). Hybrid search provides the best recall: it catches both conceptually related documents and exact-term matches.

Most modern vector databases support hybrid search natively. In Weaviate, for example, you can combine vector search with BM25 in a single query. In Qdrant, hybrid search is available through the fusion operator.

### Re-Ranking Strategies

The initial retrieval step (vector or hybrid search) returns a candidate set of memories. Re-ranking refines this set by scoring each candidate more carefully, typically using a more computationally expensive model.

#### Cross-Encoder Re-Ranking

A cross-encoder model processes the query and each candidate document together (rather than independently, as a bi-encoder does), producing a relevance score. Cross-encoders are more accurate than bi-encoders because they can attend to the interaction between query and document — but they are slower because they must process each pair individually.

Common cross-encoder models:
- **BGE-reranker**: Open-source, strong performance, available in base and large variants.
- **Cohere rerank**: Proprietary API with strong multilingual support.
- **Jina-reranker**: Open-source model optimized for reranking.

A typical re-ranking pipeline retrieves the top 50 candidates with fast vector search, then re-ranks them with a cross-encoder to produce the final top 5:

```python
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

def rerank(query: str, candidates: list[str], top_k: int = 5):
    """Re-rank candidates using a cross-encoder model."""
    reranker = CrossEncoder('BAAI/bge-reranker-base')
    pairs = [[query, doc] for doc in candidates]
    scores = reranker.predict(pairs)
    # Sort by score descending and return top_k
    ranked = sorted(zip(candidates, scores), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
    return [doc for doc, score in ranked[:top_k]]
```

#### LLM-Based Re-Ranking

For maximum flexibility, you can use an LLM to score relevance. This is the most expensive approach but allows you to encode complex relevance criteria that a cross-encoder cannot capture:

```python
import json

def llm_rerank(query: str, candidates: list[str], llm, top_k: int = 5):
    """Re-rank candidates using an LLM."""
    doc_list = "\n".join(f"[{i}] {doc}" for i, doc in enumerate(candidates))
    prompt = (
        f"Rate each document's relevance to the query on a scale of 1-10.\n"
        f"Query: {query}\n\n"
        f"Documents:\n{doc_list}\n\n"
        f"Return only a JSON array of scores, one per document."
    )
    response = llm.invoke(prompt)
    scores = json.loads(response.content)
    ranked = sorted(zip(candidates, scores), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
    return [doc for doc, score in ranked[:top_k]]
```

Reserve LLM-based re-ranking for applications where retrieval quality is critical and the cost is justified. For most applications, cross-encoder re-ranking provides sufficient quality at a fraction of the cost.

### Query Expansion and Transformation

The quality of retrieval depends heavily on the quality of the query. Agents often generate queries that are too narrow, too broad, or poorly formulated for effective retrieval. Query transformation techniques improve retrieval by reformulating the query before search.

#### Multi-Query Retrieval

Generate multiple query variants from the original query, retrieve for each, and merge the results. This is effective because different formulations capture different aspects of the information need.

```python
from langchain.retrievers import MultiQueryRetriever

# Generate 3 query variants and retrieve for each
retriever = MultiQueryRetriever.from_llm(
    vector_store.as_retriever(),
    llm=llm,
    n_queries=3
)
results = retriever.invoke("How do I handle authentication errors?")
```

#### HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings)

Generate a hypothetical answer to the query, then use that answer as the retrieval query. The idea is that a hypothetical answer will be semantically closer to the actual relevant documents than the original query.

```python
def hyde_retrieval(query: str, llm, vector_store):
    """Retrieve using Hypothetical Document Embeddings."""
    # Generate a hypothetical answer
    hypothetical = llm.invoke(f"Write a detailed answer to: {query}")
    # Use the hypothetical answer as the retrieval query
    results = vector_store.similarity_search(hypothetical.content, k=5)
    return results
```

#### Step-Back Prompting

Generate a more abstract, higher-level query that captures the broader context. This is useful when the original query is too specific and misses relevant but less directly related documents.

```python
def step_back_retrieval(query: str, llm, vector_store):
    """Retrieve using step-back prompting."""
    # Generate a broader query
    step_back = llm.invoke(
        f"Given the question '{query}', generate a broader, "
        f"more abstract question that captures the general topic."
    )
    # Retrieve using both the original and the step-back query
    results_original = vector_store.similarity_search(query, k=3)
    results_broad = vector_store.similarity_search(step_back.content, k=3)
    # Merge and deduplicate
    seen = set()
    merged = []
    for doc in results_original + results_broad:
        if doc.page_content not in seen:
            seen.add(doc.page_content)
            merged.append(doc)
    return merged
```

### Context-Aware Retrieval

Retrieval should not be blind to context. The agent's current situation — its conversation history, the user's profile, the task at hand — should influence which memories are retrieved.

#### Session-Aware Retrieval

Incorporate recent conversation turns into the retrieval query. This helps the retrieval system understand references, pronouns, and implicit context:

```
Original query: "What about the pricing?"
Context-aware query: "What are the pricing options for the enterprise plan? "
                    "(based on previous discussion about enterprise features)"
```

#### User-Profile-Aware Retrieval

Incorporate user preferences and history into retrieval. A memory system that knows a user prefers concise responses can prioritize memories about brevity; a system that knows a user is a beginner can prioritize foundational memories over advanced ones.

#### Temporal Awareness

Weight recency in retrieval scores. Recent memories are often more relevant than old ones, especially for agents that track evolving state. This can be implemented by boosting the scores of recent memories or by filtering to a recency window.

## Memory Compression and Summarization

As an agent operates over time, its memory grows. Without compression, storage costs increase, retrieval slows, and irrelevant memories dilute retrieval quality. Compression and summarization reduce memory size while preserving the information the agent needs.

### Lossy vs. Lossless Compression

**Lossless compression** preserves the original text exactly. Techniques include token-level deduplication (removing identical or near-identical chunks) and structural compression (storing only the differences between similar memories). Lossless compression reduces storage but does not reduce the number of embeddings or the retrieval search space.

**Lossy compression** discards information to achieve greater reduction. Summarization is the primary lossy technique: replace a detailed memory with a concise summary that captures the essential information. Lossy compression reduces both storage and retrieval complexity, but it risks losing details the agent might need later.

The choice between lossy and lossless depends on the application. For agents that need precise recall (e.g., a legal research agent), lossless compression is safer. For agents that need broad knowledge (e.g., a customer support agent), lossy compression via summarization is more practical.

### Summarization Techniques

#### Extractive Summarization

Extractive summarization selects the most important sentences from the original text and concatenates them. The advantage is fidelity: the summary contains only words from the original, so it cannot introduce factual errors. The disadvantage is that extractive summaries are often longer than abstractive ones and may not flow well.

Common extractive methods:
- **TextRank**: Graph-based ranking of sentences by importance.
- **LexRank**: Similar to TextRank but uses cosine similarity instead of overlap.
- **LLM-based selection**: Use an LLM to score and select the most important sentences.

#### Abstractive Summarization

Abstractive summarization generates new text that captures the essence of the original. It produces shorter, more natural summaries but can introduce errors or omit important details.

For agent memory, LLM-based abstractive summarization is the most practical approach:

```python
def summarize_memory(text: str, llm):
    """Create an abstractive summary of a memory."""
    prompt = (
        f"Summarize the following text in 2-3 sentences, "
        f"preserving all key facts and decisions:\n\n"
        f"{text}\n\n"
        f"Summary:"
    )
    response = llm.invoke(prompt)
    return response.content
```

#### Hierarchical Summarization

For long-running agents, hierarchical summarization maintains summaries at multiple levels of granularity:

1. **Raw memories**: Full-text interactions, stored temporarily.
2. **Session summaries**: Condensed summaries of each conversation session.
3. **Topic summaries**: Cross-session summaries organized by topic.
4. **Core knowledge**: Highly distilled facts and patterns that the agent always has available.

This approach mirrors the hierarchical memory architectures discussed in Chapter 2. Raw memories are compressed into session summaries after each session; session summaries are periodically consolidated into topic summaries; topic summaries are distilled into core knowledge.

### Memory Consolidation

Consolidation is the process of maintaining memory quality over time by removing redundancy and merging related memories.

#### Deduplication

Near-duplicate memories waste storage and confuse retrieval. Deduplication identifies memories with high embedding similarity and removes or merges them:

```python
def deduplicate_memories(memories: list[dict], threshold: float = 0.95):
    """Remove near-duplicate memories based on embedding similarity."""
    embeddings = np.array([m['embedding'] for m in memories])
    keep = [True] * len(memories)
    for i in range(len(memories)):
        if not keep[i]:
            continue
        for j in range(i + 1, len(memories)):
            if not keep[j]:
                continue
            similarity = np.dot(embeddings[i], embeddings[j]) / (
                np.linalg.norm(embeddings[i]) * np.linalg.norm(embeddings[j])
            )
            if similarity > threshold:
                keep[j] = False  # Keep the earlier one, remove the later
    return [m for m, k in zip(memories, keep) if k]
```

#### Merging

Related memories can be merged into a single entry. For example, if the agent has separate memories about a user's preferred programming language and their preferred framework, these can be merged into a single memory about the user's technical preferences.

#### Tiered Storage

Move older memories to cheaper, slower storage. Recent memories (last few days) stay in the fast vector database; older memories (weeks to months) move to a document store with periodic summarization; very old memories (months to years) are compressed into topic summaries.

## Practical Implementation

This section brings together the techniques discussed above into practical guidance for building and operating agent memory systems.

### Building a Memory System from Scratch

A minimal viable memory system requires four components:

1. **An embedding model** to convert text to vectors.
2. **A vector database** to store and query vectors.
3. **A retrieval pipeline** to find relevant memories.
4. **A compression layer** to manage memory growth.

Here is a complete example that combines vector search, hybrid retrieval, and re-ranking into a single pipeline:

```python
import chromadb
import numpy as np
from openai import OpenAI
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

class AgentMemory:
    """A complete agent memory system with vector search and re-ranking."""
    
    def __init__(self, collection_name: str = "agent_memory"):
        self.openai = OpenAI()
        self.chroma = chromadb.Client()
        self.collection = self.chroma.get_or_create_collection(
            name=collection_name,
            metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"}
        )
        self.reranker = CrossEncoder('BAAI/bge-reranker-base')
    
    def _embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]:
        """Compute embedding using OpenAI."""
        return self.openai.embeddings.create(
            model="text-embedding-3-small",
            input=text
        ).data[0].embedding
    
    def store(self, text: str, metadata: dict = None):
        """Store a memory with embedding and metadata."""
        embedding = self._embed(text)
        mem_id = f"mem_{self.collection.count()}"
        self.collection.add(
            documents=[text],
            embeddings=[embedding],
            metadatas=[metadata or {}],
            ids=[mem_id]
        )
        return mem_id
    
    def retrieve(self, query: str, k: int = 5, rerank: bool = True) -> list[str]:
        """Retrieve relevant memories with optional re-ranking."""
        query_embedding = self._embed(query)
        # Initial retrieval: get more candidates than needed for re-ranking
        n_candidates = k * 5 if rerank else k
        results = self.collection.query(
            query_embeddings=[query_embedding],
            n_results=min(n_candidates, self.collection.count())
        )
        
        documents = results["documents"][0]
        
        if rerank and len(documents) > k:
            # Re-rank with cross-encoder
            scores = self.reranker.predict([[query, doc] for doc in documents])
            ranked = sorted(zip(documents, scores), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
            return [doc for doc, _ in ranked[:k]]
        
        return documents[:k]
    
    def consolidate(self, threshold: float = 0.95):
        """Deduplicate memories based on embedding similarity."""
        if self.collection.count() < 2:
            return 0
        
        results = self.collection.get()
        embeddings = np.array(results["embeddings"])
        ids = results["ids"]
        
        remove_ids = []
        for i in range(len(ids)):
            if ids[i] in remove_ids:
                continue
            for j in range(i + 1, len(ids)):
                if ids[j] in remove_ids:
                    continue
                sim = np.dot(embeddings[i], embeddings[j]) / (
                    np.linalg.norm(embeddings[i]) * np.linalg.norm(embeddings[j])
                )
                if sim > threshold:
                    remove_ids.append(ids[j])
        
        if remove_ids:
            self.collection.delete(ids=remove_ids)
        return len(remove_ids)
```

This implementation provides a working memory system that you can extend with additional features: metadata filtering, hybrid search, summarization-based compression, and temporal awareness.

### Integration with Agent Frameworks

Most agent frameworks provide built-in memory abstractions that simplify integration:

**LangChain** offers `VectorStoreRetriever` for basic vector search, `MultiQueryRetriever` for query expansion, and `ContextualCompressionRetriever` for combining retrieval with document compression. These can be composed into sophisticated pipelines:

```python
from langchain.retrievers import ContextualCompressionRetriever
from langchain.retrievers.document_compressors import LLMChainExtractor

# Base retriever
base_retriever = vector_store.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 10})

# Compressor that extracts relevant passages
compressor = LLMChainExtractor.from_llm(llm)

# Combined: retrieve 10, compress to relevant passages
compression_retriever = ContextualCompressionRetriever(
    base_compressor=compressor,
    base_retriever=base_retriever
)
```

**LlamaIndex** provides `VectorStoreIndex` for vector-based retrieval and `RetrieverQueryEngine` for combining retrieval with generation. Its `QueryPipeline` abstraction allows you to chain multiple retrieval and transformation steps.

**MemGPT** and **Letta** provide built-in hierarchical memory with automatic management. If you are building a long-running conversational agent, these frameworks handle much of the memory complexity out of the box.

### Performance Optimization

As your memory system grows, performance becomes a concern. Here are the key optimization strategies:

1. **Batch embedding**: Compute embeddings in batches rather than one at a time. Most embedding APIs support batch inputs, and batch processing reduces per-document latency by 5-10x.

2. **Embedding caching**: Cache embeddings for memories that are retrieved frequently. If a memory's text does not change, its embedding does not need to be recomputed.

3. **Index tuning**: For HNSW indexes, increase `ef_search` for higher accuracy (at the cost of latency) or decrease it for faster queries. For very large collections, consider IVF or PQ indexes.

4. **Asynchronous operations**: Perform embedding computation and vector store writes asynchronously so they do not block the agent's main loop.

5. **Connection pooling**: Reuse database connections rather than creating new ones for each operation. This is especially important for cloud vector databases where connection establishment has latency.

6. **Result limiting**: Always limit retrieval results to fit within the context window. Retrieving more memories than the agent can use wastes compute and degrades response quality.

7. **Periodic consolidation**: Run deduplication and summarization on a schedule (e.g., daily) rather than on every write. This amortizes the cost of consolidation.

## Summary

This chapter covered the implementation techniques that turn memory system architecture into working code:

- **Vector-based memory** requires choosing the right embedding model (text, code, or multimodal), selecting a vector database that matches your scale and filtering needs, configuring the appropriate similarity metric and search algorithm, and designing a chunking strategy that preserves semantic coherence.

- **Retrieval techniques** go beyond simple vector search. Hybrid search combines semantic and keyword matching for better recall. Re-ranking with cross-encoders improves precision. Query expansion and transformation (multi-query, HyDE, step-back) help the agent find memories even when its initial query is imperfect. Context-aware retrieval incorporates conversation history, user profiles, and temporal information.

- **Memory compression and summarization** manage the inevitable growth of agent memory. Extractive and abstractive summarization reduce memory size while preserving essential information. Deduplication removes redundancy. Hierarchical consolidation organizes memories at multiple levels of granularity.

- **Practical implementation** involves assembling these components into a coherent system, integrating with agent frameworks, and optimizing for performance. The example code provides a starting point that you can adapt to your specific needs.

The techniques in this chapter are the building blocks for the advanced topics covered in Chapter 4: multi-agent memory sharing, memory debugging and evaluation, and emerging directions in the field. Understanding these implementation details is essential for making informed decisions about which techniques to combine and how to tune them for your specific application.

> **Key Insight**: There is no universal best configuration for agent memory. The right combination of embedding model, vector database, retrieval strategy, and compression technique depends on your agent's domain, scale, and performance requirements. Start simple — a basic vector store with cosine similarity and recursive chunking — and add complexity (hybrid search, re-ranking, summarization) only when you have measured evidence that it improves your agent's performance.
